claims.text: Elevated-temperature stress–strain, thermal-expansion, and elastic responses in HfNbTaTiZr are controlled by temperature-activated dislocation mechanisms.
Temperature-activated dislocation mechanisms reduce the influence of lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Increasing temperature to approximately 900°C increases atomic mobility in HfNbTaTiZr.
Increased atomic mobility facilitates dislocation climb in HfNbTaTiZr.
Increased atomic mobility facilitates dislocation cross-slip in HfNbTaTiZr.
The initial alloy is a well-annealed, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloy with homogeneous elemental distribution.
The initial alloy has a BCC or related structure at room temperature.
Heating activates additional slip systems through dislocation climb and cross-slip.
High temperature reduces dislocation pinning associated with local lattice distortions.
Thermally enhanced dislocation climb and cross-slip decrease yield strength relative to room temperature.
The elastic modulus decreases as temperature rises from room temperature to approximately 900°C.
The thermal-expansion coefficient increases with temperature relative to the room-temperature baseline.
The increase in thermal expansion is caused by weaker effective interatomic bonding at elevated temperature.
Thermally assisted dislocation motion delays the onset of strain hardening.
No phase transformation is expected between room temperature and approximately 900°C under the proposed conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies from room temperature to approximately 900°C at a quasi-static strain rate of about 10^-3 s^-1.
At more extreme temperatures or very high strain rates, phase transformations or dynamic recrystallization may dominate the response.
